lesson.title: Identity and inverses

lead.text: Undoing a machine means reversing its steps in the opposite order. Take a machine that triples a number and then subtracts 4, and suppose it gave back 11. The last step was the subtraction, so undo that first: add 4 to get 15. The step before was the tripling, so divide by 3 to get 5. Check by running forwards: 5 tripled is 15, and 15 less 4 is 11.

This is the socks and shoes of the last lesson. To undo putting on socks and then shoes, you take off the shoes first. The reversing machine is called the inverse of the original, and for a matrix A the inverse is written A⁻¹.
Doing a machine and then its inverse leaves every input where it started. That only works if the original machine can be undone, and some cannot. We meet those later in the lesson.
Work backwards through the machine. The last step comes off first.

reveal.text: You undid the adding first and the doubling second: 17 − 3 = 14, and half of 14 is 7.

lead.text: Before looking for inverses, meet the machine that does nothing. The identity matrix has ones down its diagonal, which runs from top left to bottom right. Every other entry is zero. For two coordinates it has rows (1, 0) and (0, 1).
Dot its rows with any input (x, y) and the first row gives x back while the second gives y, so it leaves every point where it was. It is written I, and I v = v for every vector v.

afterFigure.text: The identity is also how an inverse is described. A machine followed by its inverse changes nothing, so A⁻¹ A = I. The same holds the other way round: A A⁻¹ = I. The picture multiplies a matrix by one that undoes it, and the product is I.

lead.text: A⁻¹ undoes whatever A does to a point.

reveal.text: Undoing A leaves every vector unchanged, which is what the identity matrix does.

lead.text: The 2 × 2 identity matrix leaves every vector as it was. Think about what undoing that would take.

reveal.text: You reasoned that undoing a map that does nothing needs no change. The identity is its own inverse.

lead.text: Some inverses can be found by thinking about what the matrix does. A matrix with entries only on its diagonal, such as rows (2, 0) and (0, 5), stretches the across values by 2 and the up values by 5. To undo a stretch you shrink by the same amount, so the inverse has the reciprocals on its diagonal: rows (1/2, 0) and (0, 1/5). A negative entry such as −4 flips the direction, and its reciprocal −1/4 flips it back.

A slide is the second kind. The matrix with rows (1, 3) and (0, 1) moves each point sideways by three times its up value, and a map of this kind is called a shear. To undo it, slide back by the same amount, which is the matrix with rows (1, −3) and (0, 1).
These two cases work entry by entry. A general matrix mixes the across and up values together, so it needs a recipe. The next screens build one.
The matrix A has rows (1, 2) and (0, 1). It slides each point sideways by twice its up value.

reveal.text: You slid back by the same amount, so the entry changes sign. The inverse of a shear is the shear in the opposite direction.

lead.text: A general matrix with rows (a, b) and (c, d) mixes the across and up values, so its inverse needs more than reciprocals. There is a short recipe. First work out the number ad − bc, which is a times d minus b times c. Next swap a and d and change the signs of b and c. Finally divide every entry by ad − bc.

Try it on the matrix with rows (4, 1) and (7, 2). Here ad − bc = 4 × 2 − 1 × 7 = 1, so the inverse has rows (2, −1) and (−7, 4). Multiplying confirms it: row 1 of A dotted with column 1 of the inverse is 4 × 2 + 1 × (−7) = 1, and the other three entries come out as 0, 0 and 1.
The division is the weak point. If ad − bc is 0 the recipe asks you to divide by zero, so there is no inverse.

workedSteps.text: Find ad − bc, from the entries a = 3, b = 1, c = 5 and d = 2.
Swap the diagonal entries and negate the other two, then divide by ad − bc.
If ad − bc were zero, this division would fail and there would be no inverse.

steps.headline: Find entry (2, 2) of the inverse of A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: Swap the diagonal entries and negate the other two, then divide by that number. What is entry (2, 2) of the inverse?

lead.text: Return to the number ad − bc and see what it means when it is 0. Take the matrix with rows (1, 3) and (2, 6), where 1 × 6 − 3 × 2 = 0. It sends (3, 0) to (3, 6), and it sends (0, 1) to (3, 6) as well. Two different inputs land on the same output.

An inverse has to take each output back to one input, and this output came from two. No machine can know which one to return, so there is no inverse. The matrix has pushed every point onto a single line, and the information about where each point started is gone.
So a 2 × 2 matrix has an inverse exactly when ad − bc is not 0. The test takes one subtraction and settles the question before any other work.

Here is why inverses matter. Suppose a machine with matrix A produced the output b, and you want the input v. The machine's work is A v = b. Apply A⁻¹ to both sides and the left side becomes A⁻¹ A v = I v = v, so v = A⁻¹ b.

Take A with rows (3, 1) and (5, 2), whose inverse has rows (2, −1) and (−5, 3). If the output was (5, 9), the input is the inverse dotted with it: 2 × 5 − 1 × 9 = 1 across and −5 × 5 + 3 × 9 = 2 up. So the hidden input was (1, 2), and A(1, 2) = (3 + 2, 5 + 4) = (5, 9) confirms it.
An inverse turns the question of what went in into a multiplication, and it works for any machine that can be undone.
A machine with matrix A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ turned a hidden input v into the output (1, −2). Undo the machine to recover v.

lesson.orientation: Undo an invertible square map and recognise when an inverse cannot exist.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A machine doubles a number and then adds 3. You never see what went in. This time the machine gave back 17, and to find the input you have to work backwards, undoing each step.

Matrices on the plane raise the same problem. A machine has moved or stretched a point, and all you hold is where it landed. To get the original point back you need a second machine that reverses the first, one that leaves the plane exactly where it began.

This lesson looks at that reversing machine and at a matrix that does nothing at all. We find a recipe for undoing any 2 × 2 matrix that can be undone. We also meet matrices that cannot, because they lose information.

intro.promise: By the end you'll undo a matrix map, and spot a matrix whose work cannot be undone.

recap.keyIdea: An inverse undoes a map: A⁻¹ A = I, the matrix that does nothing. A 2 × 2 matrix has an inverse when ad − bc is not 0, and then A v = b is solved by v = A⁻¹ b.

blocks.text: Back at the machine that gave 17, undoing meant reversing the steps in the opposite order. You found that the identity is its own inverse and built the inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix. You also recovered a hidden input.

recap.nextHook: Recovering an input with an inverse is one way to solve equations, and the formula gets heavy for larger systems. The next lesson solves them with a routine you can run by hand, row by row.

questions.prompt: A machine doubles a number and then adds 3, and it gave back 17. What number went in?
hints: The machine did two things. Undo them in the opposite order.
Undo the adding first.
Take away the added amount, then undo the doubling.

misconceptions.feedback: That only undoes the adding. The doubling has to be undone as well.

questions.onCorrect: 7. You undid the last step first, then the one before it. An inverse map does just that.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A⁻¹ A = I: undoing A leaves every vector unchanged.

hints: The inverse undoes A. What is left when nothing happens?

misconceptions.feedback: A⁻¹ undoes A, so nothing of A is left. The result leaves every vector unchanged.
The zero matrix would send every vector to zero. Undoing a map leaves vectors as they were.

questions.onCorrect: Undoing A leaves every vector unchanged, which is what the identity matrix does.

questions.prompt: What is entry (1, 1) of the inverse of the 2 × 2 identity matrix?
hints: What does the identity matrix do to a vector?
Undoing a map that does nothing requires no change.
The inverse is the identity again. Read off its diagonal.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The identity is its own inverse, so the entry is 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is an off-diagonal entry. The identity's diagonal entries are the ones.

questions.onCorrect: The identity does nothing, so undoing it does nothing: it is its own inverse.

acceptedIdeas: The formula divides by ad − bc, and you cannot divide by zero.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The inverse is built by dividing by ad − bc, which fails when it is zero.

questions.prompt: Why is there no inverse when ad − bc = 0?

choices.label: The formula divides by ad − bc, and you cannot divide by zero.
A matrix with a zero entry never has an inverse.
The zero matrix cannot be multiplied.

hints: Look at the last step of the formula.

misconceptions.feedback: Many matrices with zero entries have inverses. The test is the number ad − bc.
Any matrices of matching shape can be multiplied. The issue is the division in the formula.

questions.onCorrect: The formula divides by ad − bc, so a zero there means no inverse.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (2, 2) of A⁻¹?
hints: Find ad − bc first.
Swap the diagonal entries and negate the others, then divide by that number.
Which diagonal entry of A lands in the position the question names?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The inverse is [(1, −1); (−1, 2)]. Multiplying it by A gives I.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a different diagonal entry. The two diagonal entries swap places.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the diagonal entries and divide by ad − bc, which is 1 here.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (1, 2) of A⁻¹?
hints: What does A do to a point? It slides it sideways.
To undo a sideways slide, slide back by the same amount.
The inverse slides the opposite way. Negate the entry in the top right of A.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. The off-diagonal entries are negated.

questions.onCorrect: Negate the off-diagonal entry: the inverse shear goes the other way.

questions.prompt: A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ and the output was (1, −2). What is the first coordinate of v?
hints: Write out what A v equals, one row at a time.
The second row gives the second coordinate of v on its own.
Put that value into the first row and solve.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second equation gives v₂ = −1. The first gives v₁ − 1 = 1, hence v₁ = 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first coordinate of the output, not of the input.

questions.onCorrect: Undo the map: the second row gives v₂ = −1, and the first row then gives v₁ = 2.

hints: Find ad − bc.

misconceptions.feedback: Work out ad − bc. A zero there means no inverse.

questions.onCorrect: ad − bc = 1 × 4 − 2 × 2 = 0, so there is no inverse.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (2, 2) of A⁻¹?
hints: The matrix scales each axis separately.
Undo a multiplication by dividing by the same number.
Take the reciprocal of the matching diagonal entry.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Undo multiplication by −2 with multiplication by −1/2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the entry of A itself. The inverse entry is its reciprocal.
The sign is missing. Undoing a negative scale is still negative.

questions.onCorrect: Undo multiplying by −2 by multiplying by −1/2. Diagonal matrices invert entry by entry.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ad − bc = 4 − 3 = 1, so the inverse is [(2, −3); (−1, 2)] and the entry is −3.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (1, 2) of A⁻¹?
hints: Find ad − bc first.
The off-diagonal entries change sign.
Negate the entry in the top right of A, then divide by ad − bc.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. The off-diagonal entries are negated.

questions.onCorrect: ad − bc is 1, and the off-diagonal entry is negated: −3.
